ELSEVIER 
Case Reports 
Sporadic Stiffman 
Syndrome in a 
Young Girl 
Vrajesh P. Udani, MD, 
Vikas R. Dharnidharka, MD, 
Ajit R. Gajendragadkar, MD, and 
Soonu V. Udani, MD 
A 14-month-old girl had experienced sudden episodes 
of breath-holding and spasms of the trunk and limb 
muscles, leading to cyanosis and loss of consciousness 
since 3 months of age. Her clinical features and elec- 
tromyography suggested Stiffman syndrome, and her 
response to high-dose diazepam and baclofen con- 
firmed the diagnosis. Stiffman syndrome is a rare 
entity, rarer still in childhood. This is the youngest case 
of sporadic Stiffman syndrome reported in literature. 
Distinguishing Stiffman syndrome from similar condi- 
tions such as Schwartz-Jampei syndrome or neuro- 
myotonia is important because administration of 
GABAergic agents (valproate, baclofen, diazepam) 
elicits a good response. © 1997 by Elsevier Science

Udani VP, Dharnidharka VR, Gajendragadkar AR, Udani 
SV. Sporadic Stiffman syndrome in a young girl. Pediatr 
Neurol 1997; 17:58- 60. 
Introduction 
The sporadic variety of Stiffman syndrome (SS) is a 
central nervous system (CNS) disease characterized by 
continuous/fluctuating muscular rigidity and painful 
spasms. Even in adults, this condition is very rare, with 
approximately 98 cases reported [1]; in children, there are 
few reports [2-4]. We report a case of childhood Stiffman 
syndrome. To our knowledge, this is the fifth such 
pediatric case reported in the literature, the youngest, and 
the first in India. 
Case Report 
A 14-month-old girl born of nonconsanguineous union experienced 
sudden episodes of breath-holding, accompanied by spasms of the trunk 
and limb muscles, leading to cyanosis and loss of consciousness. The 
child was normal at birth, and neither the mother nor the pediatrician had 
noticed any stiffness. The episodes had onset at 3 months of age, 
becoming more frequent with time, and were precipitated by crying, 
obstinacy, injury, and respiratory infection and were markedly reduced in 
sleep. For several months, her neck movements had been restricted, and 
she had manifested dysphagia for several months. The child achieved 
head control at 5 months and had sat at 9 months, but at 14 months of age, 
she was not walking. There was no family history of similar illness. She 
had received all appropriate immunizations. 
The child was 70 cm tall, weighed 7.5 kg, and had a head circumfer- 
ence of 42 cm, a short neck, and a partial cleft lip. Facies were not 
dysmorphic, and there were no bony or joint abnormalities. Risus 
sardonicus, blepharospasm, mild trismus, and restriction of neck move- 
ments were apparent. Stridor, with pooling of secretions, was present, 
probably due to coughing difficulty secondary to chest wall tightness. 
Posterior pharyngeal examination led to life-threatening respiratory 
muscle spasms. The child's posture showed slight flexion of the neck and 
upper trunk with extension and pronation of upper limbs. All muscles 
manifested sustained contractions, especially the chest, abdomen, and 
shoulder girdle. The appearance was that of an "infant Hercules." When 
she walked at 2 years of age, her gait was slow and waddling. No muscle 
weakness was noted. The rest of the neurologic system was normal, 
including deep tendon reflexes, 
Routine hematologic and biochemical investigations were normal, 
except for moderate anemia. Specifically, fasting and postprandial blood

glucose levels were normal. Serum creatine kinase (CK) level assessed 
elsewhere was 263 IU/L (normal 6 to 60 IU/L), and an electromyogram 
(EMG) had shown "myotonic discharges" and full recruitment of 
normal motor units. A limited repeat EMG study we performed demon- 
strated complex repetitive discharges and continuous normal motor unit 
activity. Because they produced life-threatening spasm, procaine block 
and other tests could not be performed. A provisional diagnosis of SS 
was made. 
In the following year, the girl was admitted to the hospital twice for 
increasing spasms with stridor, precipitated by respiratory infections. Her 
hospital course was complicated by pneumonia, chronic hypercarbia, and 
three episodes of respiratory arrest with bradycardia, requiring bag and 
mask ventilation or emergency tracheal intubation. Hypertension was 
observed during the first hospital stay, but subsequently resolved with 
treatment. She failed to respond to carbamazepine and intravenous 
phenytoin, but responded dramatically to high-dose diazepam and ba- 
clofen. During her second hospital stay, the child developed mild 
rhabdomyolysis after a cardiorespiratory arrest. Valproate and steroids 
added to her treatment regimen led to sustained improvement. During 
4-year follow-up in the outpatient department, the child's spasms have

resolved, although mild stiffness of the lower leg/abdominal/chest/girdle 
muscles with restriction of neck movements have persisted and the 
stiffness increases with exercise or sleep deprivation. A repeat EMG 
performed recently demonstrated no continuous motor unit activity, 
although respiratory muscle spasms could still be provoked by the 
procedure. The child was maintained on high-dose diazepam, baclofen, 
and valproate until 1 year ago. At present, she receives no medications. 
She is fully ambulant and attends normal school. 
Discussion 
SS was first described by Moersch and Woltman in 
1956 [1]. It is an extremely rare and unusual disorder 
occurring mainly in adults, characterized by gradual onset 
of stiffness/rigidity of muscles and painful spasms, which 
are chronic and fluctuating. The stiffness affects the trunk 
and abdominal muscles first and thdn the limbs. Gait is 
usually stiff and waddling. Spasms are induced by emo- 
tional/sensory stimuli or sudden movement and are re- 
duced by sleep, general and local block anesthesia, and 
drugs that potentiate GABA(~-aminobutyric acid)ergic 
transmission in the CNS such as diazepam and baclofen 
[5 ]. Involvement of facial and jaw muscles is occasionally 
reported [4]. 
EMG demonstrates continuous motor unit activity in- 
distinguishable from normal voluntary contraction. Our 
patient had a clinical picture almost identical to the 
characteristic features described and fit the modified 
diagnostic criteria [ 1 ]. Unusual features in our case include 
the presence of mild trismus and blepharospasm. In Table 
1, our case is compared with the three reported childhood 
cases. 
Clinically, very few disorders resemble SS. Dystonic 
spasms are characterized by athetoid posturing and are not 
triggered by sensory stimuli; life-threatening respiratory 
muscle spasm is not a feature of such spasms. Tetanus is 
clinically similar, except that in most cases it evolves 
acutely and resolves in a few weeks. In the very rare 
chronic form, the course does not fluctuate and improves 
with time; trismus is marked [6]. Our child's fluctuating 
course in a 3-year period, with two severe episodes 
separated by a 1-year interval, along with the absence of 
injury and history of full immunization makes the diagno-

sis of tetanus extremely unlikely. Autosomal dominant 
congenital SS always presents maximally at birth, with 
improvement occurring through infancy, and is character- 
ized by increased and abnormal startle response [7]. Our 
patient had no family history of SS, was normal at birth 
(until 3 months of age), and was maximally symptomatic 
between the ages of 1 and 3 years, On EMG, continuous 
motor unit activity is also evident in peripheral nerve 
disorders such as Schwartz-Jampel syndrome and Isaacs

syndrome (neuromyotonia) [8]. Neuromyotonia presents 
with cramps, stiffness, fasciculations, myokymia, and 
myotonia, which persist during sleep and do not respond to 
general or local anesthesia and are abolished only by 
curare [8]. Schwartz-Jampel syndrome is a hereditary 
disorder in which joint contractures, bony abnormalities, 
and markedly short stature are associated with stiffness of 
both limb and facial muscles. Unlike in SS, carbamazepine 
and phenytoin are very effective in treatment of both these 
conditions [8]. 
The pathophysiology of SS remains uncertain. Clinical and 
pharmacologic evidence suggests that the continuous motor 
unit activity is due to impaired spinal/suprasegmental inhib- 
itory systems mediated through GABA [9]. This supposition 
is supported by the fact that drags that enhance GABAergic 
inhibitory transmission, such as valproate, diazepam, and 
baclofen, are effective treatment in SS. Autoantibodies 
against -~-amino decarboxylase (GAD), a CNS enzyme 
involved in the synthesis of GABA from glutamic acid, are 
present in 30 to 60% of SS patients [8,10]. SS is also 
associated with other autoimmune diseases, especially insu- 
lin-dependent diabetes mellitus (IDDM). Although we may 
hypothesize that the anti-GAD antibodies are directly respon- 
sible for this dysfunction in GABAergic systems, they are 
present in 70% of all persons with IDDM [5], most of whom 
do not have stiffness. 
Benzodiazepines and other drags that facilitate GABA 
transmission, such as VPA, baclofen, and vigabatrin are 
useful in treatment of SS. Steroids and other immuno- 
modulating therapies such as plasmapheresis, azathio- 
prine, and intravenous IgG have anecdotally been reported 
to be effective [1,5].
